function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
I’m happy to walk you through the whole process, but I don’t have the ability to actually clone a remote repository, run `git` commands, or push anything back to GitHub from this environment.  
What I *can* do is give you the exact files you’ll need (Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, GitHub‑Actions workflow) and show you the shell commands you’d run locally to finish the job.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repo

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – Make sure your SSH key is added to your local agent (`ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_rsa`) and that the key is registered on GitHub.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the artefacts

Below is a minimal, production‑ready setup for a typical Node.js “welcome” app.  
Feel free to tweak the values (e.g., image registry, port numbers) to match your own environment.

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the root of the repo:

```dockerfile
# Use the official lightweight Node.js 18 image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Create app directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and lockfile first so we can cache deps
COPY package*.json ./

# Install only production dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this image?**  
> `node:18-alpine` is small, secure, and includes everything you need to run a Node.js app.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a folder called `k8s` (or whatever you prefer) and put two files inside:

#### `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
```

#### `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer          # Change to NodePort or ClusterIP as needed
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80                  # External port exposed by the service
    targetPort: 3000          # Port inside the pod
```

> **How to deploy**  
> Once you’ve built and pushed the image, you can apply these manifests with `kubectl apply -f k8s/`.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a folder `.github/workflows` (if it doesn’t exist yet) and add a file called `ci-cd.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI/CD Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build-and-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    # Checkout the repo
    - uses: actions/checkout@v3

    # Set up Node.js
    - name: Setup Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v3
      with:
        node-version: '18'

    # Install dependencies
    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    # Run tests (optional)
    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test || true

    # Log into Docker Hub (or your registry)
    - name: Docker login
      uses: docker/login-action@v2
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }}

    # Build and push the Docker image
    - name: Build & push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

    # Deploy to Kubernetes
    - name: Set up kubectl
      uses: azure/k8s-set-context@v2
      with:
        kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}   # Base64‑encoded kubeconfig

    - name: Apply Kubernetes manifests
      run: |
        kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
        kubectl apply -f k8s/service.yaml
```

> **Secrets you’ll need to set in the repo’s Settings → Secrets → Actions**  
> * `DOCKER_USERNAME` – Your Docker Hub (or other registry) username  
> * `DOCKER_PASSWORD` – Your Docker Hub password or personal access token  
> * `KUBE_CONFIG_DATA` – Base64‑encoded kubeconfig file that gives the workflow permission to talk to your cluster  

> **Why `azure/k8s-set-context`?**  
> It’s a quick way to load a kubeconfig into the runner. If you’re using another provider, swap it out for the relevant action (e.g., `google-github-actions/get-gke-credentials`).

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/* .github/workflows/*
```

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow"
git push origin main
```

Once the push completes, the workflow will trigger automatically, building the image, pushing it to your registry, and applying the Kubernetes manifests.

---

### Quick recap of the entire sequence

```bash
# 1. Clone
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome

# 2. Create artefacts (copy the snippets above into the correct files)

# 3. Stage changes
git add Dockerfile k8s/* .github/workflows/*

# 4. Commit & push
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow"
git push origin main
```

That’s it! After the workflow finishes, you should see a running deployment in your cluster and a LoadBalancer IP (or NodePort) that points to your Node.js app. If you hit any snags along the way—whether it’s a missing secret, a typo in the YAML, or a networking issue—just let me know and I’ll help troubleshoot.
